text: A tabletop exercise is a structured walkthrough of a hypothetical incident scenario, run with the real IR team, where no real system is touched and nothing is actually broken. It's a rehearsal of everything the last three lessons just built -- the plan, the playbooks, and the RACI matrix -- against a scenario nobody saw coming.

A facilitator runs the session without playing a response role themselves. They open with a scenario -- say, a file server encrypted on a Friday afternoon -- and then introduce injects: new pieces of information dropped in as the exercise goes, forcing the team to apply the plan and playbooks to a development nobody had time to prepare for.

Picture that exact scenario: ransomware encrypts a file server Friday at 5 p.m. The playbook says isolate and check backups, but an inject reveals the most recent backup job actually failed silently eleven days ago. Another inject reveals the on-call contact list still lists a phone number for someone who left the company two months ago. A third surfaces real confusion -- two people both believe they're Accountable for approving contact with a ransomware negotiator, because that RACI line was never actually finalized.

None of those three gaps would surface just by re-reading the plan on paper. The backup gap only shows up when someone actually checks the job log mid-exercise. The contact gap only shows up when someone actually tries to dial the number. The RACI gap only shows up when two people both reach for the same decision at once.

That's the entire value of a tabletop: it finds gaps in the plan and playbooks while there's still time to fix them, and it builds the team's familiarity with their own roles, at a cost nowhere close to what learning the same gaps during a real incident would cost. A debrief afterward -- an after-action review -- feeds straight back into updating the plan, the playbooks, and the RACI matrix.

With the plan written, the playbooks ready, the roles assigned, and now tested against a realistic scenario, Chapter 2's preparation work is done. Chapter 3 picks up with detection and analysis at real incident scale, starting with Lesson 9: triage, when it's not just a single alert anymore.
